data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction is about intended vs observed semantics: RFC 9110 'safe' means the method is *intended* not to cause server-side effects (a design-time contract), while 'idempotent' means the *observable result* of n invocations equals one invocation (a runtime property). An append-only log requires the runtime property (idempotence) of its writers, not the design-time contract (safety), because the append method is explicitly intended to cause an effect\u2014the log's correctness depends on the effect being the same on replay, not on there being no effect at all.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If RFC 9110 defines both as behavioral rather than one as intentional, this framing is wrong.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the problem demands only the formal algebraic distinction, the intentional/behavioral framing may be seen as extraneous.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Safety is a design contract (method author declares intent: no side effects). Idempotence is a behavioral property (observable equivalence under repetition). These are different kinds of statements. The log needs the behavioral guarantee; it does not need\u2014and cannot have\u2014the design contract since append is meant to change state. This resolves the apparent tension: safe \u2282 idempotent because design-time no-effect trivially satisfies behavioral equivalence, but the log only needs the behavioral half.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
